blocks.text: The market stall, the primary school down the road, the refuse skip and the naming of a street — these are not decided in Aso Rock. They are the business of the third tier of government, the local government council, whose chairman is the public official most people in a Nigerian town can actually point to.

blocks.title: Local government
blocks.text: The third tier of government, constitutionally guaranteed by section 7 of the 1999 Constitution, which establishes democratically elected local government councils. It is the level of administration closest to the people, charged with the functions listed in the Fourth Schedule. Nigeria currently has 774 local government areas: 768 councils plus six area councils in the Federal Capital Territory.

blocks.markdown:
### Functions and importance

The **Fourth Schedule** lists the main functions: collection of rates, radio and television licences; establishment and maintenance of cemeteries, burial grounds and homes for the destitute; licensing of bicycles, trucks, canoes, wheelbarrows and carts; establishment, maintenance and regulation of slaughter houses, markets, motor parks and public conveniences; construction and maintenance of roads, streets, street lighting, drains, parks, gardens and open spaces; naming of roads and streets and numbering of houses; provision and maintenance of public conveniences, sewage and refuse disposal; registration of births, deaths and marriages; assessment of privately owned houses for the purpose of levying rates; control and regulation of out-door advertising, movement and keeping of pets, shops, kiosks, restaurants and bakeries; licensing of shops and control of the sale of liquor. Local governments also participate in the provision of primary education, primary health care and agricultural extension, in so far as the state government assigns those tasks.

**Importance.** Local government brings administration within walking distance of the citizen; it is a training ground for future state and national leaders; it allows services to match local needs; it encourages participation and grassroots democracy; and it relieves the higher tiers of minor but necessary work.

items: **Statutory allocation** from the Federation Account — the largest source, paid through the State Joint Local Government Account under section 162(6).
**State grants and shares of state revenue** voted by the State House of Assembly.
**Rates** on property and tenements, assessed by the council.
**Licences, fees and fines** — market stalls, radio/TV licences, bicycle and cart licences, liquor licences, parking, birth and death registration.
**Commercial ventures** — motor parks, shops, transport services, where they exist and actually yield a surplus.
**Loans and donor funds** — borrowing (subject to law) and grants from development partners.
**Internally generated revenue (IGR)** is typically small; over-dependence on statutory allocation is itself a problem.

blocks.markdown:
### The 1976 local government reform

Before 1976, local administration was a patchwork: native authorities in the North, different council systems in the East and West, and frequent use of appointed **sole administrators**. The **1976 Local Government Reform**, issued as *Guidelines for Local Government Reform* under the Murtala/Obasanjo military government, created a **uniform, single-tier, multi-purpose** system for the whole country.

Key features: elected councils (originally a mix of elected and nominated members, later fully elective); a defined population range; a standard list of functions; federal **statutory allocation** to local governments for the first time, so they were no longer wholly dependent on the states; and the creation of **301** local government areas. Subsequent military and civilian adjustments raised the number; the 1999 Constitution lists **774**.

rows: Governors dissolve elected councils, appoint caretaker committees, and control the State Joint Local Government Account so that statutory funds do not arrive intact
Inflated contracts, ghost workers and diversion of allocation at council and state level
Shortage of trained staff, weak accounting, and chairmen who treat the council as a personal estate
Rates and licences are under-collected, so councils collapse when federal transfers are delayed
Councils become tools of the state ruling party rather than of the local community
Primary education and primary health are shared with the states, so each tier blames the other for failure
blocks.caption: Persistent problems of Nigerian local government since 1976

blocks.title: Section 7 versus practice
blocks.text: Section 7 says the system of local government by democratically elected councils is guaranteed. In practice, many states have run unelected caretaker committees for years. That gap between the text and the practice is exactly the sort of evaluation examiners reward.

blocks.title: Placing the 1976 reform on a timeline
blocks.prompt: Explain how local government in Nigeria changed in 1976 and why the 774 councils of today still face the problems the reform tried to solve.

steps.text: Before 1976: native authorities and regional council systems, often run by appointed sole administrators, with no uniform law and no direct federal allocation.
1976 reform: uniform single-tier councils, elective principle, defined functions, federal statutory allocation, 301 local governments created.
After 1976: successive increases in number, entrenchment in the 1979 and 1999 Constitutions (section 7 and the Fourth Schedule), current total 774 including FCT area councils.

The remaining problems are not a failure of the 1976 design so much as a failure of later practice: the joint account lets states intercept funds; caretaker committees undo the elective principle; corruption and weak staff waste what does arrive.
Evaluation: the reform created the legal third tier; making it financially and politically independent of the states is unfinished business.

blocks.answer: 1976 replaced a patchwork of native authorities with a uniform elected system, federal allocation and 301 councils (now 774). The design still stands in section 7, but state interference, the joint account, corruption and weak capacity prevent it from working as intended

blocks.title: 774, 1976, section 7, Fourth Schedule
blocks.text: Those four tags unlock most local-government questions. 1976 is the reform year; 774 is the current number of councils; section 7 is the guarantee of elected councils; the Fourth Schedule is the list of functions. Statutory allocation is the main revenue; rates and licences are the main local sources. Do not write that local governments create their own army or print currency.

points: Local government is the third tier, guaranteed by section 7, with functions in the Fourth Schedule, and 774 councils including the FCT area councils.
It provides grassroots services — markets, local roads, refuse, primary health and primary education participation — and trains future leaders.
Revenue comes mainly from Federation Account statutory allocation, plus state grants, rates, licences, fees and some commercial ventures.
The 1976 reform created a uniform, elected, multi-purpose system and introduced federal allocation; 301 councils then, 774 now.
Current problems include state interference and caretaker committees, the joint account, corruption, poor capacity and over-dependence on federal transfers.
